<meta>continues from previous page: while workers vaporize waters</meta>they ought to have taken, they instead took <term>pyrite</term> <gloss>iron disulfide</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term> <gloss>sulfur</gloss>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials in which there is no alchemical operation. These are expensive items from the shops, yet in our labor they are of no value at all. Truly our matter is bought from no shop; instead, it is found there daily, and hucksters throw it into the streets. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the matter of our <term>Stone</term> <gloss>the Philosophers' Stone</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor. For our Stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term> <gloss>the quicksilver of the wise</gloss>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>copper acetate</gloss>, <term>saltpeter</term> <gloss>nitre</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and infinite other things of that kind. Yet it is not dug out from wild and field-covered mountains with hammers and other instruments. Only from our mountains and springs is our Stone extracted: in our <term>Salt-spring</term> <gloss>Salis-fonte</gloss> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> are poured out, and not from those wild, foreign, and field-covered mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all this, nor can they believe or comprehend it. For the Lord has darkened and blocked their senses, wherefore they used those things otherwise than they ought to have done, and did not aim at the target at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. Namely, while they ought to have <term>distilled</term> <gloss>purified by evaporation</gloss> gently, they instead <term>sublimated</term> <gloss>vaporized with heat</gloss> with a strong fire, parched <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>corrosive acids like nitric acid</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. While they also ought to have <term>dissolved</term>, they instead <term>coagulated</term> <gloss>solidified</gloss>, and again, as people unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and repeatedly asserted with lying words that the art is not true, but false; in this, however, they themselves deservedly lie. For their own ignorance has basely deceived them, which must be imputed to their own obscure and foggy cleverness, while, according to their obscure understanding, they interpreted the words differently than they sounded. For example, while the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> <gloss>reducing to powder by heat</gloss> (which they call grinding), then those unskilled <term>pseudo-philosophers</term> <gloss>Philosophastri</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Whenever also the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <gloss>nasutuli; literally 'big-noses'</gloss> burned nature with <term>strong water</term>, and by that same water, which has no

<summary>The author explains that the true matter of the Stone is a common substance found everywhere for free, rather than the expensive minerals bought in shops. He criticizes unskilled workers for misinterpreting alchemical terms and using excessive heat or corrosive acids that destroy the natural process.</summary>
<keywords>matter of the stone, mercury, sulphur, salt, distillation, sublimation, strong waters, calcination, pseudo-philosophers, alchemical errors</keywords>
